questions.question: Under Article 239 of the Constitution, a Union Territory is administered by:

options.text: the Governor of an adjacent State

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**the President of India**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Under **Article 239** of the Constitution of India, Union Territories are administered by the President of India through an administrator appointed by him/her.
 
• The President appoints an administrator or Lieutenant Governor for each Union Territory, who acts as the executive head of the Union Territory.
 
• The **President** of India has the ultimate authority over Union Territories, making administrative decisions and delegating powers to the appointed administrators.
 
• Union Territories are governed directly by the **Central Government** unlike states which have their own elected governments. This ensures a centralized form of administration.
 
• **Examples:** Union Territories like Delhi, Puducherry, and Jammu & Kashmir have a special status with elected legislative assemblies, but their administrators still report to the President of India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Union Territories of India:**

 
 
• India currently has **8 Union Territories**, including Delhi, Puducherry, Chandigarh, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Ladakh, and Jammu & Kashmir.
 
• They are directly governed by the **Central Government**, unlike states which have their own governments.
 
• Some Union Territories, like Delhi and Puducherry, have legislative assemblies but their powers are limited compared to states.
 
 
 
• **Role of Administrator/Lieutenant Governor:**
 
 
• Administrators or Lieutenant Governors act as the representatives of the **President of India** in Union Territories.
 
• They oversee the administration, law enforcement, and implementation of policies directly from the **Union Government**.
 
• In Union Territories with legislative assemblies, the administrator/Lieutenant Governor acts in coordination with the elected government but retains significant powers.
 
 
 
• **Article 239:**
 
 
• Article 239 provides the constitutional framework for the governance of Union Territories.
 
• The **President** may appoint an administrator for Union Territories or delegate certain powers to the administrator for efficient administration.
 
• The administrator functions under the President's direct supervision and guidance.
 
 
 
• **Special Status Union Territories:**
 
 
• Union Territories like **Delhi** and **Puducherry** have legislative assemblies, allowing them to make laws on certain subjects.
 
• However, the administrator/Lieutenant Governor plays a critical role as they act on behalf of the President and can override decisions in specific circumstances.
 
• The governance of these Union Territories is a unique blend of centralized and decentralized administration.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Union Territories without Legislative Assemblies:**

 
 
• Union Territories like **Chandigarh**, **Lakshadweep**, and **Andaman and Nicobar Islands** are governed entirely by administrators appointed by the President without any legislative assembly.
 
• Their policies and administration are directly influenced by the **Central Government**.
 
 
 
• **Role of Central Government:**
 
 
• The Union Territories are supervised and funded by the **Union Government**, ensuring uniform administration across the country.
 
• They are often used as strategic locations for governance, security, and development purposes.
 
 
 
• **Governance Framework:**
 
 
• The governance of Union Territories follows a centralized approach but ensures flexibility for those with legislative assemblies like Delhi and Puducherry.
 
• This framework allows the President to maintain control while delegating administrative powers to local representatives.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• Union Territories were created to ensure efficient governance of regions that were either too small to be states or had strategic importance.
 
• Examples include **Chandigarh**, a planned city serving as the capital of two states (Punjab and Haryana).

questions.question: Which body is entrusted with recruiting India’s civil servants on the basis of merit?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The Union Public Service Commission**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC)** is India's premier central recruiting agency responsible for conducting examinations to select civil servants based on merit.
 
• Established under **Article 315 of the Constitution of India**, the UPSC is an autonomous body that ensures impartial recruitment of candidates to the civil services.
 
• The UPSC conducts various exams such as the **Civil Services Examination (CSE)**, which selects candidates for prestigious services like the IAS, IPS, IFS, and others.
 
• The Commission functions independently and is protected under the Constitution to ensure that its operations remain unbiased and free from political influence.
 
• The headquarters of the UPSC is located at **Dholpur House, New Delhi**, and it plays a critical role in recruiting candidates for various posts under the Central Government.
 
• The recruitment process includes **preliminary exams, mains exams, and a personal interview** to ensure that the candidates meet the high standards required for civil services in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **UPSC Constitutional Provisions:**

 
 
• The UPSC is governed by **Articles 315 to 323** of the Indian Constitution, which outline the structure, functions, and independence of the Commission.
 
• The Commission consists of a **Chairman and other members** appointed by the President of India.
 
• The term of office for UPSC members is **six years or until the age of 65 years**, whichever is earlier.
 
 
 
• **Functions of UPSC:**
 
 
• Conducting examinations for appointments to the civil services of the Union, including the Indian Administrative Service (IAS), Indian Police Service (IPS), and Indian Foreign Service (IFS).
 
• Advising the President and Governors on matters related to recruitment, transfers, promotions, and disciplinary actions of civil servants.
 
• Ensuring fair and transparent recruitment processes for various Group A and Group B posts under the Central Government.
 
 
 
• **Historical Background:**
 
 
• The UPSC traces its origins to the **Public Service Commission established in 1926** under British rule.
 
• Post-independence, the Commission was reconstituted as the Union Public Service Commission in **1950**, following the adoption of the Indian Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Examinations Conducted:**
 
 
• Some of the major exams conducted by UPSC include the **Civil Services Examination (CSE)**, **Indian Engineering Services (IES)**, **Indian Forest Services (IFoS)**, **Combined Defense Services (CDS)**, and more.
 
• The exams are highly competitive, with lakhs of candidates appearing every year for a limited number of posts.
 
 
 
• **Significance of UPSC:**
 
 
• UPSC ensures **merit-based selection**, promoting efficiency and integrity in the governance of the country.
 
• It plays a pivotal role in strengthening the administrative structure of India by recruiting highly qualified and competent individuals.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **UPSC vs State Public Service Commissions:**

 
 
• While UPSC handles recruitment for central civil services, **State Public Service Commissions (SPSC)** conduct exams for state-level administrative posts.
 
• Both are independent constitutional bodies, but their jurisdiction differs based on the level of governance.
 
 
 
• **Autonomy and Accountability:**
 
 
• The independence of UPSC is safeguarded to ensure unbiased recruitment, but it remains accountable to the Parliament and the President of India.
 
• The Commission submits an **annual report** to the President, detailing its activities and recommendations.
 
 
 
• **UPSC Examination Process:**
 
 
• The Civil Services Examination consists of three stages: **Prelims, Mains, and Interview**.
 
• Preliminary exams test general knowledge and aptitude, while the mains focus on specialized subjects. The interview assesses personality and decision-making capabilities.

questions.question: Which renewable energy source is dependent on the gravitational pull of the moon?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tidal energy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Tidal energy** is a form of renewable energy that is generated by the movement of tides. It is directly influenced by the **gravitational pull of the moon and the sun** on Earth's water bodies.
 
• The gravitational forces between the Earth and the moon create periodic rise and fall in sea levels, known as tides. These tidal movements are harnessed to generate electricity using tidal energy technologies.
 
• Tidal energy systems typically use **tidal barrages, tidal fences, or tidal turbines** to capture the kinetic and potential energy of moving water caused by tides.
 
• Unlike solar and wind energy, tidal energy is highly **predictable and consistent**, as tides follow a natural and regular cycle due to celestial mechanics.
 
• The implementation of tidal energy systems is most feasible in areas with a high tidal range or strong tidal currents, such as estuaries and coastal regions with significant differences between high and low tides.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Wind energy:**

 
 
• Generated using wind turbines that convert the kinetic energy of wind into electrical energy.
 
• Unlike tidal energy, wind energy is dependent on atmospheric conditions and wind patterns.
 
• Wind energy is intermittent as it relies on the availability of wind, which can vary significantly.
 
 
 
• **Biomass energy:**
 
 
• Derived from organic materials such as wood, agricultural residues, and animal waste.
 
• It is produced by burning biomass or converting it into biofuels, such as ethanol or biodiesel.
 
• Unlike tidal energy, it is not directly influenced by celestial gravitational forces.
 
 
 
• **Solar energy:**
 
 
• Harvested using photovoltaic cells that convert sunlight into electricity.
 
• It is dependent on the availability of sunlight, making it intermittent in nature.
 
• Solar energy is not connected to the gravitational pull of the moon.
 
 
 
• **Examples of tidal energy plants:**
 
 
• The **La Rance Tidal Power Station in France** is one of the oldest and largest tidal power plants in the world.
 
• The **Sihwa Lake Tidal Power Station in South Korea** is another significant facility that generates tidal energy.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Impact:** Tidal energy systems can influence local ecosystems, especially if tidal barrages alter water flow, salinity, or sedimentation patterns. However, they emit no greenhouse gases during operation, making them environmentally cleaner compared to fossil fuels.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Tidal Range:** The difference in height between high and low tides is referred to as the tidal range. Locations with a high tidal range are more suitable for tidal power generation.
 
• **Cost and Challenges:** Tidal energy systems have high initial installation costs, and their construction can face geographical and environmental challenges.
 
• **Global Potential:** According to estimates, the global potential of tidal energy is significant, with regions such as the Bay of Fundy in Canada and the Severn Estuary in the UK being prime sites.
 
• **Advantages:** Tidal energy is renewable, predictable, and environmentally friendly with low greenhouse gas emissions.
 
• **Future Prospects:** Technological advancements in tidal energy systems are expected to improve efficiency and reduce costs, making it a more viable option for clean energy generation in the future.

• India's border areas, especially in the Himalayas, require specialized equipment to counter threats effectively. Zorawar is a strategic asset in such regions.
 
• The light tank enhances India's defense posture and ensures readiness against potential threats in high-altitude areas.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

questions.question: The inaugural edition of India's first major naval exercise 'AIKEYME' was held off the coast of which African country in April 2025?

• **AIKEYME** is India's first major naval exercise in Africa, aimed at strengthening maritime collaboration and security.
 
• The inaugural edition of AIKEYME was held off the coast of **Tanzania** in **April 2025**, marking a significant milestone in India's naval outreach to Africa.
 
• Tanzania's strategic location along the Indian Ocean makes it a crucial partner for India in enhancing maritime security and fostering bilateral relations.
 
• The naval exercise focused on combating **piracy, illegal trade, and maritime threats**, ensuring the safety of international sea lanes.
 
• The initiative is part of India's broader strategy to establish a stronger presence in the Indian Ocean Region (IOR) and engage with African nations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Tanzania:**

 
 
• Tanzania is located in East Africa and bordered by the Indian Ocean to the east.
 
• Its capital is **Dodoma**, while its largest city and port is **Dar es Salaam**, which plays a pivotal role in regional maritime trade.
 
• Tanzania has a coastline stretching over **1,424 kilometers**, making it a key player in maritime security in the region.
 
• It is a member of regional organizations such as the **East African Community (EAC)** and the **Indian Ocean Rim Association (IORA)**.
 
 
 
• **India-Africa Maritime Relations:**
 
 
• India has been actively engaging with African nations to enhance maritime cooperation under initiatives like **SAGAR (Security and Growth for All in the Region)**.
 
• India aims to build capacity and strengthen the maritime infrastructure of African nations to ensure regional stability.
 
• Joint naval exercises like AIKEYME provide a platform for sharing expertise, improving interoperability, and addressing mutual challenges such as piracy and illegal fishing.
 
 
 
• **Indian Ocean Region (IOR):**
 
 
• The IOR is strategically vital for global trade, with approximately **80% of global oil trade** passing through its sea lanes.
 
• India has a vested interest in maintaining peace and security in the region, given its dependency on maritime trade.
 
• Through bilateral and multilateral efforts, India collaborates with countries like Tanzania to secure the IOR against threats like terrorism and trafficking.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Naval Exercises:**
 
 
• Naval exercises enhance the operational capabilities of participating nations and foster mutual trust.
 
• They provide opportunities for joint training, sharing best practices, and improving response mechanisms to maritime threats.
 
• Such initiatives highlight India's commitment to international collaboration and its role as a responsible global player in maritime security.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• Tanzania's location along the Indian Ocean places it at the crossroads of major shipping routes, connecting Africa, Asia, and Europe.
 
• Its proximity to key maritime chokepoints like the **Mozambique Channel** underscores its importance in regional security dynamics.
 
• India has been providing support to Tanzania in areas like defense training, capacity building, and infrastructure development to enhance its maritime capabilities.

• Collaborative efforts among nations can mitigate risks associated with piracy, smuggling, and geopolitical tensions in maritime regions.

questions.question: In 2025, which city in France hosted the French Open tennis tournament?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Paris**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **French Open**, also known as **Roland Garros**, is one of the four Grand Slam tennis tournaments and is held annually in Paris, France.
 
• The tournament is conducted at the **Stade Roland Garros**, a tennis venue named after the French aviator Roland Garros, located in Paris.
 
• It is the premier clay court tennis championship in the world and is renowned for its challenging surface and prestigious status in professional tennis.
 
• The French Open usually takes place during late May and early June every year, attracting players and spectators from across the globe.
 
• **Paris** has been the host city of the French Open since its inception in **1891**, making it an integral part of the city's rich sporting and cultural history.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Grand Slam Tournaments:**

 
 
• The Grand Slam tournaments include the **Australian Open**, **French Open**, **Wimbledon**, and the **US Open**.
 
• The French Open is distinct for being the only Grand Slam played on **clay courts**.
 
• It is considered one of the most physically demanding tournaments due to the slow and high-bouncing clay surface.
 
• Winning the French Open is a major achievement in tennis, and many legends like **Rafael Nadal**, **Chris Evert**, and **Steffi Graf** have excelled on its courts.
 
 
 
• **Stade Roland Garros:**
 
 
• Located in the **16th arrondissement of Paris**, Stade Roland Garros is the venue for the French Open.
 
• It includes multiple courts, with **Court Philippe Chatrier** being the main stadium where key matches, including finals, are played.
 
• In recent years, the stadium has undergone renovations, including the addition of a retractable roof on Court Philippe Chatrier.
 
 
 
• **Clay Courts:**
 
 
• Clay courts are made of crushed brick, shale, or stone and provide a slower playing surface compared to grass or hard courts.
 
• Players need exceptional stamina, patience, and skill to excel on clay.
 
• Rafael Nadal is widely known as the **"King of Clay"**, having won the French Open a record number of times.
 
 
 
• **Paris as a Sporting Hub:**
 
 
• Paris is a global city known for hosting major international sports events, including the **Summer Olympics** (1900, 1924, and upcoming in 2024).
 
• It is also home to top-tier football clubs like **Paris Saint-Germain (PSG)** and historic venues such as the **Stade de France**.
 
• The city’s blend of history, culture, and sports makes it a favorite destination for tourists and sports enthusiasts.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Significance:**

 
 
• The French Open began as a national tournament in **1891** and became an international event in **1925**.
 
• It is named after **Roland Garros**, a pioneer aviator and war hero, reflecting the French tradition of honoring national figures.
 
• The tournament has grown into one of the most prestigious events in tennis, with millions of viewers worldwide.
 
 
 
• **Tourism in Paris:**
 
 
• The French Open attracts thousands of visitors annually, boosting tourism and the local economy in Paris.
 
• Fans often combine the tournament with visits to iconic Parisian landmarks such as the **Eiffel Tower**, **Louvre Museum**, and **Notre-Dame Cathedral**.

questions.question: Which novel macrolide antibiotic, highlighted in a December 2024 PIB factsheet, is being positioned as India’s first indigenous drug against community‑acquired pneumonia?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Nafithromycin**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Nafithromycin** is India's first indigenous macrolide antibiotic developed for treating **community-acquired pneumonia (CAP)**.
 
• The drug was highlighted in a **December 2024 PIB factsheet**, showcasing its importance in addressing respiratory tract infections.
 
• Community-acquired pneumonia is a common infectious disease caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi, and Nafithromycin demonstrates potent activity against bacterial pathogens responsible for CAP.
 
• Nafithromycin belongs to the macrolide class of antibiotics, which are effective in targeting bacterial infections by inhibiting protein synthesis in pathogens.
 
• This development marks a significant milestone in India's pharmaceutical industry, showcasing **research and development capabilities** in antibiotic innovation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Macrolide Antibiotics:**

 
 
• Macrolides are a class of antibiotics that inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit.
 
• They are commonly used to treat respiratory tract infections, skin infections, and sexually transmitted diseases.
 
• Examples include **erythromycin, azithromycin, and clarithromycin**.
 
 
 
• **Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP):**
 
 
• CAP is an infection of the lungs acquired outside of healthcare settings.
 
• It is commonly caused by pathogens such as **Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae**, and atypical bacteria like **Mycoplasma pneumoniae**.
 
• Symptoms include cough, fever, chest pain, and difficulty breathing.
 
• Treatment typically involves antibiotics, and Nafithromycin provides a targeted solution for bacterial CAP.
 
 
 
• **Other Antibiotics in the Options:**
 
 
• **Pretomanid:** An antibiotic used for the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.
 
• **Lefamulin:** Approved for treating community-acquired bacterial pneumonia, but it is not indigenous to India.
 
• **Delafloxacin:** A fluoroquinolone antibiotic used for acute bacterial skin infections and CAP, but it is developed internationally.
 
 
 
• **India's Pharmaceutical Advancement:**
 
 
• India is globally recognized as a hub for generic medicine production and is now making strides in developing novel drugs.
 
• The development of Nafithromycin signifies India's commitment to strengthening its **healthcare infrastructure** and promoting local innovation.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Role of Indigenous Antibiotics:**

 
 
• Indigenous antibiotics like Nafithromycin reduce dependency on imported medicines and foster self-reliance in healthcare.
 
• They help address antimicrobial resistance by introducing novel mechanisms of action.
 
 
 
• **Antibiotic Resistance:**
 
 
• Antibiotic resistance is a major global health concern caused by overuse or misuse of antibiotics.
 
• New antibiotics, like Nafithromycin, are crucial in combating resistant bacterial strains.
 
• Global initiatives such as the **WHO's Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance** aim to tackle this challenge.

questions.question: Who were the Voharikas in the judicial structure of the Magadha period?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lawyer-Judges**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Voharikas** were a class of judicial officers during the **Magadha period**, who acted as **lawyer-judges**. They were responsible for resolving legal disputes and administering justice.
 
• They were well-versed in the **legal codes** and laws of the time and interpreted them to deliver fair judgments.
 
• The term "Voharika" is derived from the word "Vyavahara," which refers to legal matters, lawsuits, or disputes, indicating their primary role in judicial proceedings.
 
• They were part of the broader judicial system of ancient India, which included various levels of courts ranging from local village assemblies to royal courts.
 
• The presence of the Voharikas highlights the **structured and organized judicial framework** that existed during the Magadha period, emphasizing the emphasis on law and order in ancient India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The Judicial System in Ancient India:**

 
 
• Ancient India had a well-developed judicial system, with a focus on **Dharma (righteousness and law)**.
 
• Legal disputes were resolved at various levels, including **village assemblies (Sabhas), guild courts, and royal courts**.
 
• The king was considered the ultimate authority in judicial matters, assisted by ministers and advisors.
 
 
 
• **Categories of Judicial Officers:**
 
 
• The Voharikas were part of a larger system of judicial functionaries, including **Pradeshtris** (investigators), **Amatyas** (ministers), and **Rajukas** (revenue officers who also acted as judges).
 
• Each officer had a specific role, ensuring that the judicial process was efficient and fair.
 
 
 
• **Role of Dharma Shastras:**
 
 
• The **Dharma Shastras** served as the legal and ethical codes, guiding the decisions of judicial officers like the Voharikas.
 
• They covered various aspects of civil, criminal, and family law, ensuring a comprehensive legal framework.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Principles during the Magadha Period:**
 
 
• Justice was based on principles of fairness, equity, and adherence to **Dharma**.
 
• Witnesses and evidence played a crucial role in judicial proceedings.
 
• Punishments were often proportional to the severity of the crime, reflecting a sense of justice and deterrence.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Option 1 - Local Tax Collectors:**

 
 
• This refers to officials responsible for collecting revenue and taxes, often known as **Karshakas** or other regional terms.
 
• They had no role in judicial matters, making this option incorrect.
 
 
 
• **Option 2 - Judges in Village Assemblies:**
 
 
• Village assemblies (Sabhas) often resolved disputes at the local level, but the Voharikas operated at a more formal judicial level, making this option incorrect.

questions.question: What is the main function of RAM in a computer?

options.text: To provide temporary storage for running programs

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To provide temporary storage for running programs**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **RAM (Random Access Memory)** is a volatile memory used by computers to temporarily store data that is actively being used or processed. It enables faster access to data compared to permanent storage devices like hard drives or SSDs.
 
• When a program or application is executed, its data and instructions are loaded into the **RAM**, allowing the processor to access them quickly. This ensures smooth functioning and faster processing of tasks.
 
• RAM does not store data permanently. Once the computer is turned off or restarted, the data in RAM is erased. This makes it different from storage devices like **hard drives** or **solid-state drives** (SSDs).
 
• The size of the RAM significantly impacts the computer’s performance. A larger RAM capacity allows more applications to run simultaneously without slowing down the system.
 
• **Dynamic RAM (DRAM)** and **Static RAM (SRAM)** are two common types of RAM. DRAM is widely used in computers as the main memory, while SRAM is faster but more expensive and is typically used in cache memory.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Option 2: To control the printer**: This statement is incorrect. Controlling external devices like printers is managed by the computer's operating system and drivers, not by RAM.
 
• **Option 3: To store permanent data**: Permanent data storage is handled by devices like **hard drives, SSDs, or optical disks**. RAM is volatile and cannot retain data after the system is turned off.
 
• **Option 4: To process graphics**: Graphics processing is primarily handled by the **GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)** or integrated graphics, not RAM. However, a portion of RAM may be allocated as video memory for integrated graphics.
 
• **Uses and Applications of RAM**:
 
 
• RAM is used in various devices, including **computers, laptops, smartphones, tablets, gaming consoles, and servers**.
 
• High RAM capacity is essential for tasks like **video editing, 3D rendering, gaming, and multitasking**.
 
• For example, modern gaming systems require at least **8GB to 16GB of RAM** for smooth performance.
 
 
 
• **Important Facts**:
 
 
• RAM speed is measured in MHz or GHz, and its efficiency is determined by its **DDR type (e.g., DDR4, DDR5)**.
 
• In 2023, DDR5 RAM is the latest and fastest version, offering better bandwidth and efficiency compared to DDR4.
 
• Leading manufacturers of RAM include **Samsung, Corsair, Kingston, and Crucial**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Volatile Nature of RAM**: RAM requires a continuous power supply to retain data. If the power is interrupted, all data stored in RAM is lost.
 
• **Relation with CPU**: RAM acts as a bridge between the storage device and the **CPU**, providing quick access to data needed for processing.
 
• **Virtual Memory**: When RAM is insufficient to handle all active tasks, the computer uses virtual memory, a portion of the hard drive, to store overflow data. This process is slower than using physical RAM.
 
• **Cache Memory**: Cache memory is a smaller and faster type of memory located inside the CPU. It works alongside RAM to enhance processing speed by storing frequently accessed data.
 
• **Future Trends**: Advanced technologies like **3D XPoint** and **ReRAM (Resistive RAM)** are being developed to improve speed, capacity, and energy efficiency in memory systems.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Gynoecium** is the **female reproductive organ** of a flower in angiosperms. It consists of one or more carpels, which are the structural units of the gynoecium.
 
• The gynoecium includes three main parts: **ovary, style, and stigma**.
 
 
• The **ovary** contains ovules, which develop into seeds after fertilization.
 
• The **style** is a tube-like structure connecting the stigma to the ovary.
 
• The **stigma** is the receptive surface for pollen grains during pollination.
 
 
 
• The gynoecium plays a vital role in **sexual reproduction** by facilitating pollination, fertilization, and seed development.
 
• It is a defining feature of angiosperms, helping ensure **successful reproduction** and species propagation.

• The androecium is the male reproductive organ of a flower, consisting of stamens.
 
• Each stamen has two parts: the anther (produces pollen) and the filament.
 
 
 
• **Stamen:**
 
 
• Stamens are part of the androecium and are responsible for producing and dispersing pollen grains.
 
• They facilitate male gamete transfer to the stigma of the gynoecium.

• Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma.
 
• Fertilization occurs when male gametes from pollen unite with ovules in the ovary.
 
• After fertilization, ovules develop into seeds, and the ovary matures into a fruit.

• Angiosperms are flowering plants that reproduce sexually through their reproductive organs (androecium and gynoecium).
 
• They are the most diverse group of plants, containing over 300,000 species.

questions.question: Who is the head of the civil administration of a district court in India?

__
 
• The **District Judge** is the head of the **district court** in India and is responsible for overseeing the functioning of the civil administration of the court.
 
• As per the **Indian Judiciary System**, the District Judge holds authority in both **civil and criminal cases** within their jurisdiction.
 
• The District Judge is appointed by the **State Government** based on eligibility criteria such as experience, qualifications, and performance in judicial services.
 
• The District Judge also supervises the work of subordinate courts in the district, ensuring proper administration and judicial efficiency.
 
• Under the provisions of the **Code of Civil Procedure (CPC)** and the **Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC)**, the District Judge has the authority to hear appeals from subordinate courts and grant decisions accordingly.
 
• **District judges** are required to ensure compliance with the laws of the land and maintain the smooth functioning of judicial processes in their respective districts.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chief Judicial Magistrate:**

 
 
• The **Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM)** is responsible for the administration of criminal cases at the district level but does not hold authority over civil cases.
 
• They handle cases that fall under the jurisdiction of the magistrate's court and are subordinate to the District Judge.
 
• The CJM is appointed under the provisions of the **Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC).**
 
 
 
• **District Collector:**
 
 
• The **District Collector** is an administrative officer responsible for the overall governance and development of the district but does not have judicial authority.
 
• They oversee revenue collection, law and order, and implementation of government schemes and policies.
 
• The position is distinct from the judiciary and falls under the **executive branch** of the government.
 
 
 
• **Registrar General of the High Court:**

• This role does not pertain to district-level courts and is confined to the administrative hierarchy of the High Court.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• **District Judges** exercise both original and appellate jurisdiction.
 
• The **appointment** and functioning of District Judges are governed by Article **233** of the Indian Constitution.
 
• They play a crucial role in ensuring justice at the grassroots level and act as a bridge between the subordinate courts and the High Court.

questions.question: Volcanoes are often found in which type of plate boundary?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Convergent and divergent boundaries**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Volcanoes are commonly found at convergent plate boundaries:** At these boundaries, one tectonic plate is subducted beneath another. The subducted plate melts due to intense heat and pressure, leading to magma formation. This magma rises to the Earth's surface, forming volcanoes. Example: The Pacific Ring of Fire is a prominent area of volcanic activity caused by convergent boundaries.
 
• **Divergent plate boundaries also host volcanic activity:** At divergent boundaries, tectonic plates move apart, creating gaps where magma from the mantle can rise and solidify. This process forms new crust and is associated with volcanic activity, particularly under oceans. Example: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is a classic site of volcanic activity at divergent boundaries.
 
• **Transform boundaries typically do not cause volcanic activity:** At transform boundaries, plates slide past each other horizontally without significant magma formation. Hence, volcanoes are rarely associated with transform boundaries.
 
• **Volcanoes are not restricted to plate boundaries:** They can also occur at hotspots, which are areas of intense heat in the mantle that melt the crust to create volcanic activity. Example: The Hawaiian Islands are formed due to a hotspot and not at any plate boundary.
 
• **Global distribution of volcanoes:** Volcanoes are concentrated in areas where tectonic activity is prominent, such as subduction zones, rift zones, and hotspots. Approximately 75% of the world's volcanoes are found in the Pacific Ring of Fire.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Convergent plate boundaries:**

 
 
• These occur where plates move towards each other, causing subduction or collision.
 
• Subduction leads to intense pressure and heat, resulting in magma formation and volcanic activity.
 
• Example: The Andes mountain range in South America is formed due to subduction of the oceanic plate beneath the continental plate.
 
 
 
• **Divergent plate boundaries:**
 
 
• These occur where plates move apart, allowing magma to rise and form new crust.
 
• Volcanoes at divergent boundaries are typically less explosive compared to those at convergent boundaries.
 
• Example: The volcanic activity along the East African Rift Valley is due to divergent boundary processes.
 
 
 
• **Transform plate boundaries:**
 
 
• These occur where plates slide past each other horizontally.
 
• Volcanic activity is generally absent due to the lack of significant magma formation.
 
• Example: The San Andreas Fault in California is a famous transform boundary with no volcanic activity.
 
 
 
• **Hotspots and intraplate volcanism:**
 
 
• Hotspots are areas of mantle upwelling that cause volcanic activity away from plate boundaries.
 
• Example: Yellowstone National Park in the USA is a hotspot known for its geothermal activity and potential for large-scale volcanic eruptions.
 
• Hotspot volcanoes can form island chains as the tectonic plate moves over the stationary hotspot, creating sequential volcanic activity.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The Pacific Ring of Fire:**

 
 
• Approximately 75% of the world's active volcanoes are located in this region.
 
• It includes subduction zones where oceanic plates sink beneath continental plates, causing frequent volcanic eruptions.
 
• Countries like Japan, Indonesia, and the Philippines are highly affected by volcanic activity in this area.
 
 
 
• **Volcanic hazards:**
 
 
• Volcanic eruptions can cause lava flows, pyroclastic flows, ashfall, and volcanic gases, posing risks to life and property.
 
• Monitoring and prediction of volcanic activity are critical for disaster management and mitigation.
 
• Organizations like the United States Geological Survey (USGS) and the Global Volcanism Program track global volcanic activity.

questions.question: What is a notable characteristic of the carvings found at the entrances of the Sanchi Stupa?

options.text: Mythical creatures like yakshas and kinnaras

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jataka story narratives**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The carvings at the entrances of the **Sanchi Stupa** prominently depict **Jataka story narratives**, which are tales of the previous lives of Lord Buddha.
 
• These narratives serve as a medium to illustrate the moral teachings and the spiritual journey of Buddha in his earlier incarnations.
 
• The carvings highlight events such as Buddha's acts of sacrifice, compassion, and wisdom, which are central themes of Buddhist philosophy.
 
• The artistic style reflects the **Mauryan and post-Mauryan era's craftsmanship**, characterized by intricate detailing and symbolism.
 
• These carvings are instrumental in spreading Buddhist teachings and are an excellent example of how art was used as a storytelling medium in ancient India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Sanchi Stupa:**

 
 
• The Sanchi Stupa is one of the oldest stone structures in India and is located in **Madhya Pradesh**.
 
• It was originally commissioned by Emperor **Ashoka** in the 3rd century BCE to house relics of Lord Buddha.
 
• The Great Stupa is surrounded by four intricately carved gateways or toranas, which depict various scenes from Buddha's life and Jataka tales.
 
 
 
• **Jataka Tales:**
 
 
• These are a collection of stories that narrate the previous lives of Buddha, where he appeared in various forms such as a king, animal, or common man.
 
• They emphasize moral lessons and virtues such as generosity, compassion, and wisdom.
 
• The tales are often used as didactic tools for teaching Buddhist philosophy and ethics.
 
 
 
• **Artistic Features of Sanchi:**
 
 
• The carvings are characterized by their **narrative style**, using visual storytelling rather than direct depiction of Buddha, as early Buddhist art avoided anthropomorphic representations.
 
• Symbols such as the **lotus, wheel, and Bodhi tree** are used to represent Buddha and his teachings.
 
• They reflect the transition from Mauryan art to the post-Mauryan period, showcasing advanced stone-carving techniques.
 
 
 
• **Other Buddhist Sites:**
 
 
• Similar carvings and Jataka story depictions can be found at sites like **Ajanta Caves** and **Barabar Caves**.
 
• These sites played a crucial role in the spread of Buddhism and its teachings across India and beyond.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Symbolism in Buddhist Art:**

 
 
• Early Buddhist art used symbols such as the **lotus flower** (purity), **wheel** (dharma), and **stupa** (enlightenment) to represent Buddha.
 
• The absence of Buddha's anthropomorphic depiction reflects the **Aniconic phase** of Buddhist art.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• Emperor Ashoka, after embracing Buddhism, played a pivotal role in the construction of stupas and spreading Buddhist teachings.
 
• The Sanchi Stupa is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognized for its historical and architectural significance.
 
 
 
• **Spread of Buddhism:**
 
 
• Art and architecture, like the carvings at Sanchi, were essential tools for the dissemination of Buddhist philosophy.
 
• These visual representations made the teachings accessible to a wider audience, including those who were illiterate.

questions.question: In 2025, which two countries were involved in renewed tensions over the South China Sea, prompting international concern about maritime security?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**China and Philippines**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **South China Sea** is a highly strategic and contentious maritime area, with several countries claiming overlapping territories.
 
• **China** has been asserting its claim over most of the South China Sea, citing its "Nine-Dash Line" policy, a position that has been widely criticized by international bodies and neighboring countries.
 
• The **Philippines**, which shares proximity to the South China Sea, has disputed China's territorial claims, particularly in areas like the Spratly Islands and Scarborough Shoal.
 
• Tensions between China and the Philippines renewed in **2025** due to activities such as the building of artificial islands, military deployment, and fishing rights violations.
 
• The dispute has prompted global concern over **maritime security**, freedom of navigation, and international trade routes in the region.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **South China Sea Overview:**

 
 
• The South China Sea spans an area of approximately **3.5 million square kilometers** and is bordered by countries such as China, the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei, and Indonesia.
 
• It is home to critical shipping lanes, with nearly **30% of global maritime trade** passing through its waters annually.
 
• Rich in resources, the region contains vast reserves of **oil and natural gas**, alongside significant fishing grounds.
 
 
 
• **China’s Territorial Claims:**
 
 
• China bases its claim on the "Nine-Dash Line," which encompasses about **90% of the South China Sea**.
 
• In **2016**, an arbitral tribunal in The Hague ruled against China's claims, favoring the Philippines in a case under the **United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)**, but China rejected the ruling.
 
• China has engaged in activities such as **building artificial islands** and deploying military bases to strengthen its presence.
 
 
 
• **Philippines’ Position:**
 
 
• The Philippines asserts sovereignty over areas like **Scarborough Shoal** and parts of the **Spratly Islands**, as recognized under international law.
 
• It has pursued diplomatic efforts and military partnerships, especially with the **United States**, to counter China's dominance.
 
• The country relies heavily on the South China Sea for **fishing and trade**, making the resolution of disputes critical to its economic stability.
 
 
 
• **Global Implications:**
 
 
• Tensions in the South China Sea affect **international trade routes**, as the region is central to Asia-Pacific economic activity.
 
• Countries like the **United States** have conducted **freedom of navigation operations (FONOPs)** to challenge excessive maritime claims and ensure open access.
 
• Regional organizations like **ASEAN** have been attempting to mediate disputes through dialogue and agreements such as the **Code of Conduct (COC)** in the South China Sea.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Context:**

 
 
• Disputes in the South China Sea date back to the **20th century**, with intensified claims emerging in the **1990s**.
 
• In **2012**, China took control of Scarborough Shoal after a standoff with the Philippines, heightening tensions.
 
 
 
• **Legal Framework:**
 
 
• The **United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)** provides guidelines for resolving maritime disputes, defining concepts such as **Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs)**.
 
• Despite its adherence to UNCLOS, China has frequently disregarded rulings, leading to global criticism.
 
 
 
• **Regional Cooperation:**
 
 
• ASEAN has sought to establish a binding **Code of Conduct** to prevent conflicts in the South China Sea, though progress has been slow due to differing national interests.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The term **'Ahara'** or **'Rashtra'** during the **Satavahana Empire** referred to a **district or administrative division**. This system was used to organize and manage the empire effectively.
 
• The Satavahanas ruled large territories in the Deccan region, and to ensure efficient administration, they divided their empire into smaller units known as **'Ahara'** or **'Rashtra'**, which were equivalent to districts.
 
• Each **Ahara** or **Rashtra** was under the control of an officer called the **Amatya** or **Mahamatra**, who was responsible for collecting taxes, maintaining law and order, and overseeing the administration.
 
• The system of administrative divisions ensured effective governance and allowed the Satavahana rulers to maintain control over their vast empire, which extended over large parts of present-day Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Karnataka.
 
• This system of governance reflects the organized and decentralized administration adopted by ancient Indian empires to manage their territories efficiently.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **The Satavahana Empire:**

 
 
• The **Satavahana Empire** was one of the most prominent dynasties in ancient India that ruled from the 1st century BCE to the 3rd century CE.
 
• Their empire primarily covered regions of the **Deccan Plateau** and extended into parts of central and southern India.
 
• The Satavahanas were known for their contributions to **art, architecture, trade, and administration**.
 
 
 
• **Administrative Practices:**
 
 
• The empire was divided into smaller administrative units like **Ahara** (district), **Grama** (village), and **Janapada** (province).
 
• Each administrative unit had designated officers who were responsible for its governance and maintenance of law and order.
 
• The officers also ensured the collection of taxes and facilitated trade and commerce within their jurisdiction.
 
 
 
• **Other Terminologies:**
 
 
• **Amatya:** These were officers responsible for the administration of the **Ahara** or **Rashtra**.
 
• **Mahamatra:** A higher-ranking officer, often responsible for overseeing multiple administrative divisions.
 
• **Rajuka:** Officials involved in judicial and administrative tasks at the local level.
 
 
 
• **Taxation and Revenue:**
 
 
• The Satavahanas had a well-organized system of taxation. Taxes were collected from agriculture, trade, and crafts.
 
• The revenue generated was used for the welfare of the people and for maintaining the army and infrastructure.
 
• Land revenue was the primary source of income, and it was often collected in the form of produce or currency.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of Satavahana Rule:**
 
 
• The Satavahanas promoted **trade and commerce** by establishing trade routes and supporting the merchant class.
 
• They issued coins made of lead, copper, and silver, which facilitated trade and strengthened their economy.
 
• Their art and architecture, such as the **Amaravati Stupa**, reflect their cultural and artistic achievements.

questions.question: Which government initiative primarily focuses on improving human development by ensuring healthcare and nutrition for women and children?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Poshan Abhiyaan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Poshan Abhiyaan**, also known as the **National Nutrition Mission**, was launched by the Government of India on **8 March 2018**, coinciding with International Women's Day.
 
• The initiative aims to address the issue of **malnutrition** among women, children, and adolescents by ensuring proper nutrition and healthcare facilities.
 
• It primarily focuses on reducing **stunting, undernutrition, anemia** (among young children and women), and low birth weight in babies, targeting children aged **0-6 years** and pregnant women.
 
• The program utilizes technology-driven solutions, such as **mobile apps and real-time monitoring systems**, to track progress and ensure effective delivery of services.
 
• Under Poshan Abhiyaan, initiatives like **Poshan Pakhwada** and **Rashtriya Poshan Maah** are implemented annually to create awareness about nutrition and promote community participation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Features of Poshan Abhiyaan:**

 
 
• The mission adopts a **multi-ministerial approach** involving ministries like Women and Child Development, Health, and Education.
 
• It is implemented in collaboration with **state governments** to ensure coverage across all districts in India.
 
• The program promotes **behavioral change** among communities through awareness campaigns, workshops, and training programs.
 
• Funds under Poshan Abhiyaan are shared between the **Central Government and State Governments** in a **60:40 ratio** (90:10 for North-Eastern states and Himalayan states).
 
• The initiative incorporates the use of **Anganwadi Workers** and **ASHA workers** to directly engage with beneficiaries, ensuring last-mile delivery.
 
 
 
• **Relevant Data:**
 
 
• India has the highest number of **malnourished children** globally, with reports showing that **35.5%** of children under the age of 5 years are stunted, as per the **National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5)** conducted in **2019-2021**.
 
• The mission targets to reduce **stunting** to **25%** by **2022**, from the baseline of **38.4%** recorded in the **NFHS-4**.
 
• It aims to reduce **anemia** among women and children by **3% annually** and ensure 100% coverage of pregnant women with supplementary nutrition.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Schemes:**
 
 
• **Digital India:** Focuses on digital empowerment of citizens and is unrelated to healthcare or nutrition.
 
• **Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao:** Aims to improve the **sex ratio** and promote **education for girls** but does not address healthcare and nutrition directly.
 
• **Skill India Mission:** Focuses on **enhancing vocational skills** for employment and is not related to nutrition or healthcare.
 
• **Poshan Abhiyaan:** Specifically targets nutrition and healthcare improvements for women and children, making it the most relevant initiative for the question.
 
 
 
• **Global Context:**
 
 
• The initiative aligns with the **Sustainable Development Goals (SDG)**, particularly **SDG 2 (Zero Hunger)** and **SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being)**.
 
• India's efforts under Poshan Abhiyaan contribute to global objectives of reducing malnutrition and improving health outcomes.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• Poshan Abhiyaan involves the use of **ICT-based real-time monitoring** to ensure transparency and accountability in service delivery.
 
• The initiative complements existing schemes like the **Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS)** and **Mid-Day Meal Scheme**, amplifying their impact.
 
• Community participation through initiatives like **Poshan Melas** and **Village Health and Nutrition Days** enhances the program's outreach and effectiveness.
 
• The **Jan Andolan** aspect of Poshan Abhiyaan aims to make nutrition a people-centric movement, encouraging grassroots involvement.
